name: Lökbatan Mud Volcano
card_summary: Lökbatan Mud Volcano is one of the world's most active, known for its powerful eruptions and a surprising connection to Azerbaijan's oil industry.
narrative: You know, this isn't just any mud volcano. Lökbatan is actually one of the top five most active in the world, erupting roughly every three to ten years. Imagine, back in 1867, one eruption sent flames 400 to 500 meters high – bright enough to read a newspaper 60 kilometers away at night. What's really interesting is its role in the oil industry. In 1933, a well drilled right here gushed 20,000 tons of oil, proving that these volcanoes don't destroy oil deposits, but actually point to them. That specific well, number 45, is still producing oil today.
retrieval: Lökbatan Mud Volcano is located 12-15km southwest of Baku, near the Lökbatan settlement, on the Caspian Sea coast. It is one of the world's five most active mud volcanoes, with recorded eruptions dating back to 1829, and has erupted approximately every 3-10 years. The volcano is a Tentative World Heritage Site and holds historical significance for confirming the genetic link between mud volcanoes and oil fields in 1933.

name: Independence Museum of Azerbaijan
card_summary: The Independence Museum tells the story of Azerbaijan's journey to sovereignty, from ancient times right up to today. It's a good place to understand the national spirit.
narrative: There was an earlier Independence Museum, founded in 1919, but it only lasted a year. This current museum opened in 1991, just as the country was regaining its independence. It started with 7,000 exhibits, now it has grown to 20,000. The museum's main goal is to trace Azerbaijan's national independence movement, covering everything from ancient history to the present day. You'll find that story laid out across six distinct halls.
retrieval: The Independence Museum of Azerbaijan was established on January 9, 1991, with 7,000 exhibits, now expanded to 20,000. Its primary objective is to highlight Azerbaijan's national independence movement from ancient times to the present, displayed across six thematic halls. The collection includes art, architecture, maps, books, and currencies.

name: Palace of the Shirvanshahs
card_summary: This 15th-century palace complex in Baku's Inner City was built by the Shirvanshahs. It's an ensemble of structures, including a mosque and burial vaults, all built in the Shirvan-Absheron style.
narrative: The Palace of the Shirvanshahs dates to around 1500, built by the Shirvanshah rulers. It's a complex of buildings in the Inner City, not just a single palace. You'll see the main building, a mosque with a minaret, and burial vaults. In the past, a wall with towers surrounded it, making it an inner stronghold of the Baku fortress. The builders relied on the Shirvan-Absheron architectural school for the whole ensemble.
retrieval: The Palace of the Shirvanshahs is a 15th-century building complex in Baku, Azerbaijan, built by the Shirvanshahs in the Shirvan-Absheron architectural style. It includes the main palace building, Divanhane, burial-vaults, a mosque with a minaret, Seyid Yahya Bakuvi's mausoleum, Murad's gate, a reservoir, and remnants of a bath house. Declared a museum-preserve in 1964 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000, it was historically the inner stronghold of the Baku fortress.
